title: The promise kept
hook: the oldest telling of the young wanderer and King Bimbisara, and what happened years later

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vangisa grieving his teacher, and your line, the poet's question. Did you write your line? Today, day six hundred, a new chapter, and a scene you first met long ago. Day six hundred.

Way back, on day forty-one, a young wanderer walked through Rajagaha with his bowl, and a king on a palace terrace couldn't stop watching him. The king offered him an army and a fortune. The young man said no. That was more than a year and a half ago on this path. Today we open the Great Chapter of the Sutta Nipata, and its first poem is that same scene, in what may be one of the oldest tellings of it we have. We'll hear it in its own plain words, and then we'll follow the story forward, to what happened when the wanderer came back. Today: the promise kept.
screen: `DAY 41: A KING ON A TERRACE.` → `THE GREAT CHAPTER OPENS.` → `THE STORY, FORWARD.`

segments.voice: The poem is the Pabbajja Sutta, the going forth. Tradition says Ananda speaks it. King Bimbisara sees a young man walking for alms, eyes lowered, looking only a plow's length ahead. He sends messengers, who find him eating on a hillside outside the city. The king drives out, steps down from his chariot, and makes the offer: you're young, noble-looking, lead my army, take wealth. The young man answers simply. My people live beside the Himalaya, he says, among the Kosalans, rich and energetic, Sakyans by birth. I didn't leave home to find pleasures. I've seen the danger in them, and the safety in letting go. I'm going to strive. That's where my heart is glad. And the poem ends there. Notice what it doesn't include. In this old poem, there's no promise to return. That comes in later tellings: the king asks him, if you find what you seek, come back and teach me first, and he agrees. And the monastic texts tell how it was kept. After awakening, the Buddha walked back to Rajagaha. The king came out to hear him with a great crowd, and understood. Then Bimbisara said that as a young prince he'd had five wishes: to be crowned, that an awakened one would come to his kingdom, that he could honor him, that he'd be taught, and that he'd understand. All five, he said, have come true today. He gave the community its first park, the Bamboo Grove. A promise made on a hillside, kept years later.
screen: `EYES LOWERED, A PLOW'S LENGTH AHEAD` · `I DIDN'T LEAVE HOME FOR PLEASURES` · `THE PROMISE COMES IN LATER TELLINGS` · `FIVE WISHES, ALL COME TRUE` · then, large: `THE PROMISE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recall day forty-one, and your own promises. Sit and settle. Picture the hillside: a young man with a bowl, a king stepping down from his chariot. Two people who would meet again. Now think of a promise someone kept to you, maybe years later than you expected. Let gratitude come. Then think of one promise you've made and haven't yet kept, small or large. Don't scold yourself. Just hold it gently, and see the first step back toward it. The bell holds the time.
The promise kept. The young wanderer refuses a king's fortune, and in later tellings promises to return; awakened, he comes back, and all five of the king's wishes come true. Today's word.
Your line: the promise kept. Take the first step today toward the promise you're still holding: a call, a date set, a start. Day six hundred.

howItsDone: Buddhists remember King Bimbisara's gift of the Bamboo Grove as the first monastery park, and pilgrims to Rajgir in India visit both the Bamboo Grove and the hills where the young wanderer is said to have met the king.

options: accept, and use it to do good.
tell him who you are and that you're going to strive.

original.note: Pali pabbajja: going forth, leaving home for the homeless life. the name of Sn 3.1.

trapdoor: what you thought: the story of the king and the wanderer is one fixed account.
what it means: the old poem tells the meeting; later tellings add the promise; the monastic texts tell how it was kept.

what a scholar hears: Sn 3.1 ends with the refusal; the request to return is in the commentarial biography, and Vinaya Mahavagga 1.22 tells of the return, the five wishes and the gift of the Veluvana.

notes: Sn 3.1 paraphrased. Confirm: the poem is traditionally attributed to Ananda; 'looking a plow's length ahead'; messengers find him on Pandava hill; the king's offer; the reply naming the Himalayan people among the Kosalans, of the Adicca clan, Sakyan by birth.
Confirm Mahavagga 1.22: the five wishes of Bimbisara, his understanding, the meal and the gift of the Veluvana.
Day 41 earlier told the scene using the later telling with the promise; this day distinguishes the layers.
'More than a year and a half ago' (day 41 to day 600) is accurate for a daily learner.
